scenario_stem:
Wychwood Furniture Co is a private limited company in Country X making flat-pack wardrobe doors and drawer fronts for 12 furniture retailers. It has traded for 8 years and employs 34 workers, including 18 on manual cutting benches. Last year the company sold 240,000 doors at $28 each, earning revenue of $6,720,000, but 6% of doors failed quality checks and were reworked at a cost of $95,000.

The managers are comparing two options. Option A is to keep hand-cutting and add a second shift. Option B is to spend $900,000 on CAM-controlled CNC routers and edgebanders, which would replace 10 cutting jobs, raise output to 300,000 doors a year and cut the defect rate to 2%. The machines would cost $120,000 a year to maintain but save $210,000 a year in wasted board.

questions.question_text: Define 'computer-aided manufacturing (CAM)'.
questions.model_answer: Computer-aided manufacturing is the use of computer-controlled machines and software to carry out production processes such as cutting and assembly, rather than doing them by hand. [2]

knowledge_max_2: CAM = use of computers and software to control manufacturing machinery and processes
CAM programs guide machines such as CNC routers and edgebanders automatically

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Wychwood Furniture Co of using CAM-controlled machines.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: CAM machines cut and edge doors to the same measurements every time, removing human error [k]. The defect rate would fall from 6% of doors to 2%, saving costly rework [app]. Benefit 2: CAM-controlled routers work continuously and faster than hand cutting [k]. Output would rise from 240,000 doors a year to 300,000, helping Wychwood serve its 12 retailers [app].

knowledge_max_2: CAM gives consistent, accurate output and removes human error
CAM machines work faster and continuously, raising output
application_max_2: Defect rate falls from 6% to 2%, cutting rework costs
Output rises from 240,000 to 300,000 doors a year for 12 retailers

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Wychwood Furniture Co could face if it buys the CAM-controlled machines.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: The machines are expensive to buy and run [k]. Option B costs $900,000 plus $120,000 a year in maintenance, a heavy outlay for one factory [app]. If sales stay flat, these fixed costs may take years to recover and strain cash flow [an]. Problem 2: CAM removes labour from the cutting benches [k]. Replacing 10 cutting jobs from 34 workers would make staff redundant [app]. Redundancy payments and lower morale among remaining workers could reduce productivity [an].

knowledge_max_2: High capital and running costs for CAM equipment
CAM machines replace manual jobs, leading to redundancies
application_max_2: Option B costs $900,000 plus $120,000 a year in maintenance
10 cutting jobs would be replaced from 34 workers
analysis_max_2: Fixed costs rise, squeezing profit and cash flow if sales do not grow
Redundancy costs and lower morale can reduce productivity and damage the workforce

questions.question_text: Do you think Wychwood Furniture Co should buy the CAM-controlled machines rather than add a second shift? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Case for Option B: CAM would make production faster and more accurate [k]. Output would rise from 240,000 to 300,000 doors a year while defects fall from 6% to 2%, and the $210,000 a year board saving less $120,000 a year maintenance still leaves about $90,000 a year before rework savings [app]. Lower unit costs would let Wychwood price competitively and win larger orders from its 12 retailers [an]. Case for Option A: keeping hand-cutting avoids the $900,000 investment and protects the 10 cutting jobs [k]. A second shift keeps 18 manual benches running with no redundancy costs, but the 6% defect rate would stay [app]. Staying manual would keep rework at $95,000 a year and leave Wychwood vulnerable to rivals with fewer defects [an]. Overall, Wychwood should buy the CAM machines because the defect saving and $210,000 annual board saving outweigh the maintenance cost and the 10 lost jobs [eval]. If retailer demand weakens, the company could lease rather than buy the machines outright [eval].

knowledge_max_2: CAM gives faster, more consistent production than hand methods
Keeping manual cutting avoids capital cost and redundancies
application_max_2: Output rises to 300,000 doors; defects fall from 6% to 2%; $210,000 board saving less $120,000 maintenance
Option A avoids $900,000 spend; $95,000 a year rework cost would continue; 18 manual benches kept
analysis_max_2: Lower unit costs improve competitiveness and retailer orders
Manual operation preserves rework cost burden and weaker quality position
evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation based on stem figures (defect saving and $210,000 outweigh costs)
Condition suggested for the alternative (lease if demand weakens)

scenario_stem:
Ondara Convenience Stores is a private limited company operating 4 convenience stores in Country X for 6 years. It employs 58 staff and earns annual sales revenue of $9.6 million. Each store relies on handwritten stock books, and a full stock-take takes 2 days per store every month. Shrinkage from theft and missing stock costs the company $84,000 a year.

The owners are comparing two options. Option A is to keep the manual system and hire 1 part-time stock clerk per store at $19,000 a year each. Option B is to spend $260,000 on EPOS tills linked to a central stock database, which scan every sale and reorder stock automatically, cutting shrinkage by 60% and reducing the monthly stock-take to 4 hours per store.

questions.question_text: Define 'electronic point of sale (EPOS)'.
questions.model_answer: Electronic point of sale is a computerised till system that scans barcodes, records each sale and updates sales and stock records automatically at the checkout. [2]

knowledge_max_2: EPOS = computerised till that records sales electronically
Linked to stock records so inventory updates automatically

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Ondara Convenience Stores of installing EPOS tills.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: EPOS records every sale instantly, so stock figures are always up to date [k]. Reordering would be automatic, replacing the 2 days per store monthly stock-take with a 4 hours per store task [app]. Benefit 2: EPOS creates a detailed sales record that helps ordering decisions [k]. Shrinkage of $84,000 a year would be expected to fall by 60%, saving about $50,400 a year [app].

knowledge_max_2: EPOS keeps stock records accurate and current in real time
Detailed sales data supports better ordering and pricing decisions
application_max_2: Monthly stock-take falls from 2 days to 4 hours per store
Shrinkage of $84,000 reduced by 60% (about $50,400 a year saved)

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Ondara Convenience Stores could face if it installs EPOS tills.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: EPOS requires a large upfront payment [k]. Option B costs $260,000, a big outlay for a business earning $9.6 million a year [app]. If the system underperforms, the money is hard to recover and cash flow suffers [an]. Problem 2: Staff must learn to use the new system [k]. With 58 staff across 4 stores, training and early till errors could frustrate customers [app]. Poor training could slow service and lose regular shoppers [an].

knowledge_max_2: EPOS needs a large upfront capital payment
Staff require training to operate EPOS correctly
application_max_2: Option B costs $260,000 against $9.6 million annual revenue
58 staff across 4 stores need retraining and support
analysis_max_2: High fixed investment reduces liquidity and financial flexibility
Disruption and customer frustration during changeover could offset savings

questions.question_text: Do you think Ondara Convenience Stores should install EPOS tills rather than hire stock clerks? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Case for EPOS: EPOS automates sales recording and reordering [k]. It would cut shrinkage by 60% (about $50,400 a year from $84,000) and turn the 2 days per store stock-take into a 4 hours per store task, while 4 clerks would cost $76,000 a year (4 x $19,000) [app]. Accurate, live stock data would help Ondara avoid empty shelves across its 4 stores [an]. Case for clerks: Option A avoids the $260,000 outlay and keeps records checked by people who know each store [k]. Four part-time clerks at $19,000 a year each would cost $76,000 a year and could also serve customers, but would not cut shrinkage or speed up tills [app]. Clerks alone leave the shrinkage problem and the 2-day stock-takes untouched [an]. Overall, Ondara should install EPOS because the $50,400 shrinkage saving plus avoided clerk costs of $76,000 a year (about $126,400 in total) recovers the $260,000 outlay in roughly 2 years [eval]. If staff are unsure about the system, the owners could trial EPOS in 1 store first [eval].

knowledge_max_2: EPOS automates sales recording and stock reordering
Manual clerks keep records but cannot prevent shrinkage electronically
application_max_2: 60% shrinkage cut (~$50,400 of $84,000), stock-take falls from 2 days to 4 hours per store
4 clerks at $19,000 each = $76,000 a year vs Option B $260,000 outlay
analysis_max_2: Live stock data reduces stockouts and over-ordering across stores
Clerks retain old problems (shrinkage, slow stock-takes), weakening the manual option
evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation using stem figures (save ~$126,400 a year, recovery in about 2 years)
Suggestion to de-risk the decision (trial in one store first)

scenario_stem:
Breckfield Pump Works is a private limited company in Country X making water pumps for farms for 11 years. It employs 85 workers and produces 1,400 pumps a month. Annual sales revenue is $11.2 million. Errors between the design office and the factory floor mean 8% of pumps need reworking before dispatch.

The directors are choosing between two options. Option A is to keep the existing separate CAD and CAM machines with 2 standalone inspection stations. Option B is to spend $2.4 million on a CIM system linking the design office, 6 CNC machines, automated scanners and the stock control database, which would cut rework from 8% to 3% and raise output to 1,750 pumps a month. Training 12 staff would cost $36,000.

questions.question_text: Define 'computer-integrated manufacturing (CIM)'.
questions.model_answer: Computer-integrated manufacturing is the linking of all production stages - design, machining, quality inspection and stock control - into one computer-controlled system that shares information automatically. [2]

knowledge_max_2: CIM links design, production, inspection and stock in one computer system
Information flows automatically between stages without manual paperwork

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Breckfield Pump Works of installing a CIM system.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: CIM shares design data directly with the machines, removing manual re-entry [k]. Rework would fall from 8% of pumps to 3%, saving materials and labour [app]. Benefit 2: Linking all stages in one system speeds up the whole production flow [k]. Output would rise from 1,400 pumps a month to 1,750 pumps a month, a 25% increase [app].

knowledge_max_2: CIM removes manual data transfer errors between design and production
An integrated flow speeds up the process from planning to dispatch
application_max_2: Rework falls from 8% to 3% of pumps
Output rises from 1,400 to 1,750 pumps a month (a 25% increase)

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Breckfield Pump Works could face if it installs a CIM system.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: CIM costs a great deal of money up front [k]. Option B requires $2.4 million plus $36,000 to train 12 staff [app]. Borrowing that sum would add interest payments and raise financial risk for the company [an]. Problem 2: CIM depends on all its linked parts working together [k]. A fault in 1 of the 6 CNC machines or in the shared database could stop the whole line [app]. One breakdown could halt deliveries to farm customers and breach supply commitments [an].

knowledge_max_2: CIM requires very high capital investment and training spend
Integrated systems can fail as a whole if one component breaks
application_max_2: Option B costs $2.4 million plus $36,000 to train 12 staff
6 CNC machines and one shared database are all linked together
analysis_max_2: High borrowing increases interest burden and financial risk
A single-point failure could stop production and lose farm customer contracts

questions.question_text: Do you think Breckfield Pump Works should install the CIM system rather than keep the separate machines? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Case for CIM: CIM links design, machining, inspection and stock in 1 system [k]. It would cut rework from 8% to 3% and raise output from 1,400 to 1,750 pumps a month, a 25% increase on $11.2 million of revenue [app]. Fewer errors and higher output would raise profit and let Breckfield take on more farm contracts [an]. Case for keeping separate machines: Option A avoids the $2.4 million cost and the $36,000 training bill [k]. The existing CAD and CAM machines and 2 inspection stations already work, so there is no disruption or retraining [app]. Staying with separate machines keeps the 8% rework rate and the 1,400 pumps a month output limit [an]. Overall, Breckfield should install CIM, because cutting rework from 8% to 3% and lifting output by 25% outweighs the upfront cost over time [eval]. The directors could phase the system in over 12 months to limit disruption [eval].

knowledge_max_2: CIM integrates all stages to cut errors and speed flow
Separate machines avoid capital cost and retraining
application_max_2: Rework falls from 8% to 3%; output rises from 1,400 to 1,750 pumps (+25%) on $11.2 million revenue
Option A avoids $2.4 million and $36,000 training; 8% rework and 1,400 pumps limit remain
analysis_max_2: Lower rework and higher output raise profit and capacity for farm contracts
Keeping separate machines preserves status quo inefficiencies and output ceiling
evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation using stem figures (rework and 25% output gain outweigh cost)
Practical phasing suggestion to reduce risk (12-month phased rollout)

scenario_stem:
Sandpiper Bakery Co is a private limited company in Country X supplying supermarket loaves for 9 years. It employs 46 staff working 6 days a week and bakes 90,000 loaves a week. Weekly fixed costs are $28,000 and total variable costs are $36,000. The wholesale price is $1.10 per loaf and hand-wrapping damages 2% of loaves every week.

The family owners are comparing two options. Option A is to keep hand-wrapping and hire 6 extra wrapping staff at $400 a week each. Option B is to buy an automated wrapping line for $720,000, which seals 140 bags a minute, halves the damage rate to 1% and replaces 9 hand-wrapping jobs earning $420 a week each. The line would need $54,000 a year in maintenance.

questions.question_text: Define 'automation'.
questions.model_answer: Automation is the use of machines and computer-controlled systems to carry out tasks previously done by people, with little or no human involvement. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Automation = machines doing tasks with little or no human input
Often computer-controlled and capable of continuous running

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Sandpiper Bakery Co of buying the automated wrapping line.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Automated wrapping machines work continuously and consistently [k]. The line seals 140 bags a minute and would halve the damage rate from 2% of loaves to 1% [app]. Benefit 2: Automation cuts the number of workers needed for wrapping [k]. Replacing 9 jobs earning $420 a week each would save $3,780 a week in wages [app].

knowledge_max_2: Automation gives consistent output and fewer damaged products
Automation replaces labour, lowering wage costs
application_max_2: Damage rate halves from 2% to 1% of 90,000 loaves a week
9 jobs at $420 a week saved = $3,780 a week

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Sandpiper Bakery Co could face if it buys the automated wrapping line.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: The line is expensive to purchase [k]. Option B costs $720,000 plus $54,000 a year in maintenance [app]. Heavy fixed outlays reduce profit in the early years and increase the risk if supermarket orders fall [an]. Problem 2: Automation would make 9 hand-wrapping workers redundant [k]. Losing 9 of 46 staff could lead to redundancy payments and lower morale among the rest [app]. The remaining team may resist the change, slowing production [an].

knowledge_max_2: Automation needs a large capital purchase and running costs
Automation makes workers redundant
application_max_2: Option B costs $720,000 plus $54,000 a year in maintenance
9 of 46 staff would lose their jobs
analysis_max_2: High fixed costs squeeze early profit and cash flow
Redundancy costs and resistance may slow production and hurt quality

questions.question_text: Do you think Sandpiper Bakery Co should buy the automated wrapping line rather than hire 6 extra wrapping staff? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Case for the automated line: automation removes human error and works faster than people [k]. It seals 140 bags a minute, halves damage from 2% to 1% of 90,000 loaves and saves $3,780 a week on 9 jobs (plus about $990 a week in avoided wasted loaves) [app]. Lower unit costs would protect Sandpiper's margins when selling at $1.10 per loaf to supermarkets [an]. Case for hiring staff: Option A keeps jobs and avoids the $720,000 purchase and $54,000 annual maintenance [k]. Six extra staff at $400 a week each cost only $2,400 a week and preserve flexibility if orders change [app]. Hand-wrapping keeps damage at 2% and delivers nowhere near the consistency of 140 bags a minute [an]. Overall, Sandpiper should buy the automated line, because $3,780 a week wage savings plus reduced waste exceed the $2,400 weekly cost of extra staff [eval]. If the family fears supermarket demand dropping, leasing the line could reduce the risk [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Automation is faster and more consistent than manual work
Manual hiring avoids capital outlay and keeps flexibility
application_max_2: Line seals 140 bags/minute, halves damage 2% to 1%, saves $3,780 a week on 9 jobs
6 staff at $400 a week = $2,400 a week; avoids $720,000 and $54,000 a year maintenance
analysis_max_2: Lower unit costs protect margins on $1.10 supermarket loaves
Manual option keeps 2% damage and weaker consistency
evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation (wage savings plus waste reduction exceed extra staff cost)
Suggestion to reduce risk (lease the line if demand is uncertain)

scenario_stem:
Sorrel & Main Fashion Co is a private limited company in Country X making school uniforms for 20 schools for 14 years. It employs 52 machinists and 3 pattern cutters who draw cutting patterns by hand. Annual revenue is $7.3 million and the company spends $900,000 a year on fabric. Hand-drawn patterns take 2 weeks to prepare and cutting waste averages 9% of fabric.

The directors are comparing two options. Option A is to keep hand-drawn patterns and train the 3 pattern cutters in better hand-cutting methods. Option B is to spend $140,000 on CAD software and 2 workstations, plus $18,000 a year in licences, which would cut pattern preparation from 2 weeks to 2 days and reduce cutting waste from 9% to 6% of fabric.

questions.question_text: Define 'computer-aided design (CAD)'.
questions.model_answer: Computer-aided design is the use of computer software to create, modify and store designs on screen instead of drawing them by hand. [2]

knowledge_max_2: CAD = software used to create and modify designs digitally
Designs are stored digitally and easily edited, reused and shared

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Sorrel & Main Fashion Co of adopting CAD.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: CAD makes patterns accurate and easy to edit on screen [k]. Pattern preparation would fall from 2 weeks to 2 days, speeding up work for 20 schools [app]. Benefit 2: CAD nests pattern pieces efficiently on screen to cut fabric waste [k]. Cutting waste would fall from 9% to 6% of fabric, saving about $27,000 a year on $900,000 of fabric [app].

knowledge_max_2: CAD improves accuracy and consistency of designs
CAD reduces material waste through efficient layouts
application_max_2: Pattern time falls from 2 weeks to 2 days across 20 schools
Waste falls from 9% to 6%, about $27,000 saved a year on $900,000 fabric spend

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Sorrel & Main Fashion Co could face if it adopts CAD.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: CAD requires money and licences [k]. Option B costs $140,000 up front plus $18,000 a year in licences, and the 3 pattern cutters would need retraining [app]. These set-up and running costs cut profit in the early years [an]. Problem 2: CAD depends on computers working [k]. If a workstation fails, pattern work stops until repaired and cutting cannot start without patterns [app]. Delays would hold up uniform deliveries to 20 schools and risk school contracts [an].

knowledge_max_2: CAD needs capital spend, annual licences and retraining
CAD output depends on working hardware and software
application_max_2: Option B costs $140,000 plus $18,000 a year in licences and 3 retrained cutters
Failure of 1 of the 2 workstations would stop all pattern work
analysis_max_2: Fixed set-up costs reduce early profit margins
System failure delays cutting, risking late deliveries and school contracts

questions.question_text: Do you think Sorrel & Main Fashion Co should adopt CAD rather than keep hand-drawn patterns? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Case for CAD: CAD creates designs on screen that can be changed instantly [k]. It would cut pattern preparation from 2 weeks to 2 days and reduce waste from 9% to 6%, saving about $27,000 a year on $900,000 of fabric [app]. Faster turnaround and less waste would raise profit on school uniform orders worth part of $7.3 million of revenue [an]. Case for hand-drawn patterns: Option A avoids the $140,000 cost and the $18,000 yearly licences [k]. The 3 pattern cutters already serve 20 schools and need no retraining or computers [app]. Hand methods keep the 2-week pattern cycle and the 9% waste rate, so savings stay slow to arrive [an]. Overall, Sorrel & Main should adopt CAD, because pattern time cut from 2 weeks to 2 days and about $27,000 a year in fabric savings outweigh licence costs [eval]. The directors could buy 1 workstation first to test staff acceptance [eval].

knowledge_max_2: CAD speeds up and improves accuracy of pattern design
Hand-drawn patterns avoid capital cost and retraining
application_max_2: Pattern time 2 weeks to 2 days; waste 9% to 6%; about $27,000 a year saved on $900,000 fabric
Option A avoids $140,000 and $18,000 yearly licences; 3 cutters serve 20 schools already
analysis_max_2: Faster turnaround and lower waste raise profit on $7.3 million revenue
Hand methods preserve slow 2-week cycle and 9% waste, limiting savings
evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation using stem figures (time and $27,000 fabric saving)
Practical low-risk first step suggested (trial one workstation)

scenario_stem:
Warrenfield Farm Shops is a private limited company running 3 farm shops in rural Country X for 7 years, selling milk, cheese, eggs and preserves. It employs 24 staff and average monthly sales revenue is $85,000 per shop. Fresh stock is ordered by hand from notebook records and 12% of fresh stock is thrown away each month as unsold waste.

The owners are comparing two options. Option A is to keep handwritten records and add 1 ordering day per week per shop. Option B is to spend $96,000 on EPOS tills with a stock-control system that tracks sales in real time and suggests reorder quantities, expected to cut fresh-stock waste from 12% to 5% of stock and shrinkage by 40%. Some loyal cash-paying customers rarely use cards.

questions.question_text: Define 'stock control'.
questions.model_answer: Stock control is the process of ordering, storing and monitoring a business's stock so it has enough to meet customer demand without holding too much. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Stock control = managing the ordering, holding and monitoring of inventory
Aim is the right stock at the right time with minimum waste

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Warrenfield Farm Shops of installing EPOS with stock control.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: EPOS records every sale as it happens [k]. Stock levels would update in real time, so notebook records are replaced and reordering becomes automatic [app]. Benefit 2: Live sales data shows exactly what sells [k]. Fresh-stock waste would fall from 12% to 5% of stock across the 3 farm shops [app].

knowledge_max_2: EPOS gives accurate, up-to-date stock records in real time
Sales data allows automated, needs-based reordering
application_max_2: Fresh-stock waste falls from 12% to 5% of stock
Real-time tracking replaces handwritten notebook records in 3 shops

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Warrenfield Farm Shops could face if it installs EPOS.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: EPOS tills cost money to buy and run [k]. Option B requires $96,000, a large sum for 3 rural shops earning $85,000 a month each [app]. The outlay may take years to recover from waste savings [an]. Problem 2: Some customers pay cash and rarely use cards [k]. EPOS could make loyal cash-paying customers feel unwelcome or unable to pay as before [app]. Lost goodwill in small rural communities could cut sales sharply [an].

knowledge_max_2: EPOS needs significant upfront and ongoing investment
EPOS may not suit customers who prefer paying cash
application_max_2: Option B costs $96,000 against 3 shops earning $85,000 a month each
Loyal cash-paying customers rarely use cards at these rural shops
analysis_max_2: High fixed outlay strains cash flow of small rural shops
Alienating cash customers risks losing loyal local sales

questions.question_text: Do you think Warrenfield Farm Shops should install EPOS rather than keep handwritten records? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Case for EPOS: EPOS links the till to live stock records [k]. It would cut monthly fresh-stock waste from 12% to 5% and shrinkage by 40% across 3 shops averaging $85,000 in sales each month [app]. Better stock data would cut waste costs and free staff from notebooks to serve customers [an]. Case for handwritten records: Option A costs nothing and keeps ordering simple for 24 staff [k]. Adding 1 ordering day per week per shop would catch waste earlier without new technology [app]. Handwritten records also keep personal contact with local suppliers, but waste would stay near 12% and shrinkage untracked [an]. Overall, Warrenfield should install EPOS, because waste falling from 12% to 5% saves far more than an extra ordering day costs [eval]. The owners could keep notebook records as backup and train staff gradually to retain loyal cash customers [eval].

knowledge_max_2: EPOS gives real-time stock visibility and automated reordering
Manual records cost nothing but keep errors and waste
application_max_2: Waste falls 12% to 5%, shrinkage cut by 40%, across 3 shops at $85,000 monthly sales each
Option A adds 1 ordering day per week per shop, no capital cost, 24 staff unchanged
analysis_max_2: Lower waste and shrinkage directly protect profit margins
Manual system leaves 12% waste and shrinkage untracked
evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation (waste saving outweighs ordering-day cost)
Suggestion to de-risk (keep notebook backup, train staff gradually)

scenario_stem:
Amberdale Dye Works is a private limited company in Country X dyeing wool and cotton yarn for knitwear factories for 10 years. It employs 30 workers who stir and heat dye vats by hand in batches of 400 kg. Output averages 60 tonnes of dyed yarn a month and annual revenue is $5.4 million. Colour shade rejects cost the business $72,000 a year.

The owners are comparing two options. Option A is to keep hand-stirring and retrain workers to improve shade matching. Option B is to spend $480,000 on mechanised vats with automatic temperature and stirring controls, cutting reject costs by 70% and saving $34,000 a year in wages by needing 2 fewer dye hands. The vats would need $45,000 a year in maintenance.

questions.question_text: Define 'mechanisation'.
questions.model_answer: Mechanisation is the use of machines to carry out tasks that were previously done by hand, with a human operator controlling or supervising them. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Mechanisation = machines replacing hand labour for specific tasks
Human operators still control or supervise the machines

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Amberdale Dye Works of mechanising the dye vats.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Mechanised vats control temperature and stirring exactly [k]. Reject costs would fall by 70%, saving about $50,400 a year from the current $72,000 [app]. Benefit 2: Machines can work longer and more evenly than hand-stirring [k]. Batches of 400 kg would be dyed more consistently, lifting output quality for knitwear customers [app].

knowledge_max_2: Machines repeat precise settings, improving consistency
Mechanisation raises output per worker and allows longer running
application_max_2: Reject costs fall 70%, about $50,400 a year saved from $72,000
400 kg batches dyed more consistently for knitwear factories

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Amberdale Dye Works could face if it mechanises the dye vats.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: Mechanised vats need heavy investment [k]. Option B costs $480,000 plus $45,000 a year in maintenance [app]. These fixed costs reduce profit and could strain cash flow for a business earning $5.4 million a year [an]. Problem 2: 2 fewer dye hands would be needed [k]. Making 2 of 30 workers redundant brings redundancy payments and possible disputes [app]. Losing experienced dye workers could hurt quality in the early months [an].

knowledge_max_2: Mechanisation requires large capital and running costs
Mechanisation reduces the number of workers required
application_max_2: Option B costs $480,000 plus $45,000 a year in maintenance
2 fewer dye hands out of 30 workers would be needed
analysis_max_2: High fixed costs reduce profit and strain cash flow
Redundancy payments and lost skills could hurt early quality and morale

questions.question_text: Do you think Amberdale Dye Works should mechanise the dye vats rather than retrain workers? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Case for mechanisation: mechanised vats deliver exact, repeatable temperature and stirring [k]. Reject costs would fall by 70% (saving about $50,400 a year) and wages would drop by $34,000 a year, giving about $84,400 of yearly savings before the $45,000 maintenance cost [app]. Net savings of about $39,400 a year plus better consistency would strengthen quality for knitwear customers [an]. Case for retraining: Option A avoids the $480,000 investment and keeps all 30 workers in jobs [k]. Retraining could improve shade matching, but rejects would not fall as far or as reliably as with automation [app]. Staying manual keeps flexibility for small batches, but the $72,000 a year reject cost largely remains [an]. Overall, Amberdale should mechanise, because about $39,400 net annual savings and 70% fewer rejects outweigh hand-stirring over time [eval]. The owners could keep 1 manual vat for delicate batches during the transition [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Mechanisation gives exact, repeatable process control
Retraining avoids capital cost and keeps jobs
application_max_2: Rejects fall 70% (~$50,400 saved), wages drop $34,000, net about $39,400 after $45,000 maintenance
Option A avoids $480,000, keeps 30 workers, but $72,000 reject cost persists
analysis_max_2: Net annual savings and consistency strengthen competitiveness with knitwear factories
Manual retraining leaves high reject costs and weaker consistency
evaluation_max_2: Clear justified recommendation (net $39,400 plus 70% reject cut outweighs retraining)
Practical transition suggestion (keep one manual vat for delicate batches)

scenario_stem:
Glen Carrick Water Co is a private limited company in Country X bottling spring water for 5 years. It employs 28 workers on 2 shifts and bottles 1.2 million litres a month, selling at $0.55 per litre. Annual revenue is $7.92 million and capping and labelling are done by hand, with 4% of bottles leaking at the cap.
